explainer.heading: What the article says
explainer.body: The Olympic motto is “Faster, Higher, Stronger”, and records keep being broken. The article asks why. Its answer: records are not mainly the result of humans becoming more able — the conditions, technology and lifestyle of athletes have changed.
explainer.example: Roger Bannister ran the first mile under 4 minutes (1954); today’s record is nearly 17 seconds faster.
explainer.hook: Records ≠ better humans; records = better conditions.

explainer.heading: Owens vs Bolt
explainer.body: Jesse Owens ran 100 m in 10.2 s in 1936 on a simple dirt track that slowed him down. Usain Bolt ran 9.58 s in 2009 on a bouncy, non-slip modern track with state-of-the-art shoes. Analysing film of Owens showed that on a modern track he would have been less than a step behind Bolt.
explainer.example: The 2016 Olympic marathon winner was 50 minutes faster than the 1896 winner.

explainer.heading: Technology in sport
explainer.body: Swimming: gutters at the sides of pools stop waves slowing swimmers; special swimsuits help too. At the 2008 Olympics, 25 world records were broken in the “Water Cube”, a pool engineers perfected to be the fastest in the world. Wearable devices record speed and heart rate, giving instant feedback so injuries can be spotted early.
explainer.example: Data at the 2016 Olympics showed Neymar did more sprints than average; he was told to slow down or get injured.

explainer.heading: Different lives
explainer.body: Bannister was a medical student who ran his record mile after a morning hospital shift. Owens spent much of his time earning money to pay university fees. Bolt had full-time training, coaches, adequate rest and his own cook. Sport has become an industry — but human desire to be faster, higher, stronger still drives it.
explainer.example: Antonym of “insufficient” in the text: adequate.

explainer.heading: Vocabulary
explainer.body: Words with more than one meaning (e.g. “record”, “track”, “match”). Adjectives vs adverbs: quick → quickly, good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard. Suffixes -able / -ic: comfort → comfortable, athlete → athletic, energy → energetic. Phrasal verbs: give up (stop trying), warm up (prepare body), back down (withdraw), take over (take control), get over (recover).
explainer.example: He runs fast. (adverb) / He is a fast runner. (adjective)

explainer.heading: Grammar: clauses
explainer.body: A main (independent) clause makes sense alone. A subordinate (dependent) clause does not; it begins with a word like because, when, who, that, if. Kinds: noun clause (works as a noun: “I know that he won”), adjective/relative clause (describes a noun: “the athlete who won”), adverb clause (tells when/why/how: “He trained hard because he wanted gold”).
explainer.example: Main: Bolt won the race. Subordinate: because he trained hard.
explainer.hook: Who/which/that after a noun → adjective clause.

explainer.heading: Writing: a story
explainer.body: A good story has a catchy title, an opening that sets the scene (who, where, when), a problem or conflict, a climax, and a resolution. Use past tenses, time words (suddenly, after that, finally), adjectives and dialogue to make it lively.
explainer.example: “As the whistle blew, Riya’s heart pounded…”

How has technology changed the way athletes train?
questions.model: Athletes wear devices that record running speed and data like heart rate. This gives instant feedback to athletes and coaches, so health problems or injuries can be found and treated quickly and performance can be improved.
points: Instant feedback → injuries found early / better performance

questions.q: Give an example from the text showing that athletes of the past led different lives.
questions.model: Roger Bannister ran his record mile after his usual morning shift at a hospital, while Usain Bolt had full-time training, coaches, rest and his own cook. (Or: Jesse Owens had to earn money for his university fees.)
points: Example of a past athlete (Bannister’s hospital shift / Owens earning fees)

questions.q: “New records in athletics are not necessarily the result of changes in human ability.” Explain with evidence from the article.
questions.model: The article compares Owens and Bolt. Owens ran on a slow dirt track; Bolt ran on a bouncy non-slip track with special shoes. Analysis showed Owens would have been less than a step behind Bolt on a modern track. In swimming, gutters and special swimsuits increased speed; 25 records fell in the Water Cube. Modern athletes also train full-time with coaches and diets, unlike Bannister and Owens. So changed conditions and technology, not just ability, explain new records.
points: Owens vs Bolt comparison (track/shoes; less than a step behind)
